extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political thinkers, and citizens concerned with democratic institutions and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and evaluative principles for designing and safeguarding political institutions in democratic (equal) societies, emphasizing protections for private independence, checks on administrative power, and the civic instruments that preserve liberty. Drawn from a chapter-level survey of the effects of equality on government and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the liberty of the press
rubrics_metrics.description: “The liberty of the press is infinitely more valuable amongst democratic nations than amongst all others; it is the only cure for the evils which equality may produce.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press freedom is the chief democratic instrument of freedom: it enables isolated individuals to appeal to the nation or to mankind, summons fellow-citizens to assistance, and counterbalances the isolating effects of equality. Example: printing accelerates equality and is one of its best correctives. Anti-pattern: neglecting press freedom because a society is 'democratic' or equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen judicial power to protect private interests
rubrics_metrics.description: “The strength of the courts of law has ever been the greatest security which can be offered to personal independence; but this is more especially the case in democratic ages.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should attend to private interests, be accessible to the humblest complainant, and provide redress for minor/private grievances. Judicial power must grow in scope and strength to keep pace with government intrusion into private life. Anti-pattern: weak or distant courts that do not prioritize routine private complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and preserve forms (procedural safeguards)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Forms become more necessary in proportion as the government becomes more active and more powerful... Nothing is more pitiful than the arrogant disdain of most of our contemporaries for questions of form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural forms act as a barrier between the strong and the weak, retard arbitrary action, and give the disadvantaged time to respond. Democratic legislators should treat even small forms with deliberate respect. Anti-pattern: dismissing procedural requirements as mere bureaucracy and abolishing them because they 'retard' action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent administrative despotism and over-centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid allowing the State to “cover the surface of society with a net-work of small complicated rules” that ‘circumscribe the will’ and reduce citizens to passive dependents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the extent of centralized administrative reach; set clear, distinct, and settled limits to government action and avoid minute uniform regulations that stifle originality and action. Design institutions to prevent the State from becoming an all-providing, all-directing tutelary power. Anti-pattern: permitting a vast, minute, and uniform administrative apparatus that manages most private concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and empower intermediate public bodies and elective local officers
rubrics_metrics.description: “A portion [of administrative powers] may be entrusted to secondary public bodies, temporarily composed of private citizens... election is a democratic expedient which insures the independence of the public officer.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitute elective public officers and local/provincial assemblies for hereditary or purely central agents to decentralize administrative power and preserve private independence. Example: county/provincial assemblies as partial substitutes for aristocratic officers. Anti-pattern: centralizing all administrative functions in a single, remote bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage voluntary associations as counterweights to the State
rubrics_metrics.description: Private citizens can combine to constitute bodies of wealth, influence, and strength corresponding to an aristocracy, defending their own rights and the common liberties of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote associations (political, commercial, manufacturing, scientific, literary) as independent, durable actors that resist arbitrary state encroachment. Associations serve as an alternative source of social power without aristocratic injustice. Anti-pattern: suppressing or neglecting civil associations so individuals remain atomized and easily oppressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect private rights and small-scale interests from being sacrificed
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of private persons among democratic nations are commonly of small importance, of recent growth, and extremely precarious—the consequence is that they are often sacrificed without regret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators and judges must be on constant alert to prevent government from lightly sacrificing private rights for supposed public utility. Even apparently minor private rights, if violated, risk corrupting public morals and endangering the whole community. Anti-pattern: justifying infringement of private rights routinely in the name of public utility or expediency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on rare electoral acts to sustain self-government
rubrics_metrics.description: “This rare and brief exercise of their free choice... will not prevent them from gradually losing the faculties of thinking, feeling, and acting for themselves.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that occasional elections and representative acts cannot substitute for everyday institutions that cultivate citizens' capacity for self-government. Design civic and institutional routines that keep citizens engaged and independent, rather than expecting infrequent elections to preserve liberty. Anti-pattern: assuming that periodic voting alone suffices to maintain a free people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about revolution and sudden change
rubrics_metrics.description: Men accustomed to frequent changes grow to prefer sudden violence and to trivialize forms; revolutionary habits can become permanent in democratic societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democratic nations have special reason to hesitate before undertaking revolutions; many grievances are better endured or remedied without violent change because revolutions engender lasting vices (contempt for forms, readiness to sacrifice private rights). Anti-pattern: normalizing revolutionary justification of rights violations as 'political necessity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Design institutions that cultivate individual strength and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to enable individual man to maintain independence, strength, and original power; 'raise him by the side of society at large, and uphold him in that position.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should focus not only on making the State or works great but on making great men: protect and foster conditions (education, civic habits, decentralized authority, associations, legal remedies) that maintain personal independence and civic virtue. Anti-pattern: building systems that produce industrious but pusillanimous and enfeebled citizens whose individuality is lost.
